title: The Duplicated Split

scenario.situation: An image classifier hits 97% accuracy on the offline test set but only 70% on live production traffic, and the discrepancy was discovered after deployment.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The Head of ML is convinced the gap is caused by distribution shift — production images look different from training images due to new camera hardware rolled out last month.
scenario.question: Is distribution shift really responsible for the 27-point accuracy gap?

decisions.prompt: The Head of ML wants you to investigate the distribution shift hypothesis. How do you frame your investigation?

options.label: Measure covariate shift between train and production
options.detail: Compute feature distribution statistics (pixel statistics, embedding distances) between training data and live production samples.
options.consequence: You find modest distributional differences consistent with new camera hardware. This confirms the hypothesis on the surface — but you've only looked where you were told to look. The offline test set was never interrogated at all.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the stakeholder's hypothesis and never questioned whether the offline benchmark was valid in the first place.

options.label: Audit the train/test split construction before accepting the 97% benchmark
options.detail: Step back and ask whether the offline metric is trustworthy: inspect how the split was built, what the unit of observation is, and whether any shared structure exists across splits.
options.consequence: You immediately find that the dataset contains multiple augmented crops from the same subjects, and the split was done at the image level — not the subject level. This opens a contamination thread the distribution-shift hypothesis would never have surfaced.

options.label: Collect more production samples and retrain the model
options.detail: Gather recent production images, add them to training data, and fine-tune the model to close the gap.
options.consequence: Retraining on production samples nudges accuracy up slightly, but the fundamental benchmark inflation is never caught. The new model will still be evaluated on a leaky split and will appear to 'work' offline again.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to remediation before diagnosing the root cause — the leaky evaluation persists.

options.label: Run error analysis on production misclassifications
options.detail: Sample and manually label production images the model got wrong to characterize the failure mode.
options.consequence: You catalog interesting failure patterns, but they look like edge cases on unfamiliar subjects — consistent with both drift AND leakage. Error analysis alone can't distinguish between the two explanations.
options.divergenceCost: Gathered useful color but couldn't distinguish leakage from drift — the root cause remains ambiguous.

decisions.prompt: Auditing the split reveals the dataset has 4,200 images of 420 distinct subjects, each with ~10 augmented variants. Which metric do you use to assess the model's true generalization?

artifact.title: Model accuracy across evaluation cuts — raw image-level split
artifact.caption: Image-level offline accuracy looks strong. Camera-era subsets are both far below it, suggesting shift — but the camera subsets track each other closely, which is suspicious if shift were the real driver.

options.label: Accuracy on the existing image-level test set
options.detail: Use the 97% figure already computed on the held-out images from the original random split.
options.consequence: The 97% benchmark stands — but it was computed on images whose subject-twins live in the training set. The model memorized identities rather than learning generalizable features, and this metric can't reveal that.
options.divergenceCost: Trusted a metric built on a contaminated split — the leakage stays invisible.

options.label: Accuracy on a subject-grouped holdout (no subject appears in both train and test)
options.detail: Regroup data by subject ID, perform a group-aware split so all images of a given subject are exclusively in train or test, and re-evaluate.
options.consequence: With subjects properly isolated, offline accuracy drops to 71% — almost exactly matching production. The 97% was entirely an artifact of near-duplicate leakage across the original split, not a signal of real model quality.

artifact.title: Model accuracy — subject-grouped split vs. original image split
artifact.caption: Once subjects are grouped before splitting, offline accuracy collapses to 71% — nearly identical to production. The gap was the benchmark, not the world.

decisions.prompt: The subject-grouped split yields 71% offline, matching production almost exactly. What do you tell the Head of ML?

options.label: "There's no distribution shift — it's purely group leakage. Rebuild the split and the problem is solved."
options.detail: Make the definitive causal call and close the investigation.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified leakage, but overstated certainty. A modest residual gap could still include some real drift. Closing the investigation now risks missing a compounding factor, and the team rebuilds the split without validating on a truly independent production holdout.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a complete explanation and skipped the validation step that would confirm it.

options.label: "Distribution shift is not the primary driver — group leakage inflated the benchmark by ~27 points. We should rebuild the split grouped by subject and validate the new benchmark against a curated production holdout before drawing final conclusions."
options.detail: Report the finding, name the mechanism, and recommend a confirmatory step.
options.consequence: You've reframed the team's mental model with concrete evidence — the gap was in the ruler, not the model's environment — and you've proposed a clean path to a trustworthy benchmark. The Head of ML can now prioritize model improvement with accurate baselines rather than chasing phantom drift.

insight: The 97% accuracy was never real — augmented crops of the same subjects leaked across the image-level train/test boundary, letting the model 'recognize' near-duplicates it had already memorized. Grouping by subject before splitting collapsed offline accuracy to 71%, perfectly matching production and eliminating the apparent distribution shift. The lesson is architectural: whenever a dataset has a natural grouping entity (subject, patient, session, document), the split must be performed at that entity level or the benchmark measures memorization, not generalization.
